screens.title: Performance Tuning Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Performance tuning is about improving how a system uses its resources so services respond faster and do more work with less waste. In this lesson you will learn what tuning is, how to change kernel parameters safely with the sysctl facility, how to set user and process resource limits, and how to give processes the right C P U priority. Rather than chasing symptoms, tuning should be driven by monitoring: measure first, change one thing at a time, and re-measure. For example, you might reduce swapping by adjusting a kernel setting so interactive applications feel snappier, or raise file-descriptor limits for a busy web server so it can accept many concurrent connections. We will walk through concrete commands, file edits that persist changes across reboots, and a simple experiment that launches a background job and adjusts its priority. I will also point out common pitfalls—like changing a kernel knob without testing—that can cause instability. By the end of the sequence you will know how to make small, reversible changes and validate their effect. Think of tuning as careful engineering rather than guesswork: measure, adjust, verify. screens.title: What is performance tuning?
screens.narratorSegment: Performance tuning is the deliberate practice of adjusting configuration and resource allocations to improve responsiveness, throughput, or efficiency. A helpful analogy is tuning a car engine: you measure how it runs, adjust a single setting like timing or fuel mixture, test the change on a drive, and then decide whether to keep it. In Linux that single setting might be a kernel parameter, a per-user limit, or a process priority. Tuning differs from troubleshooting: troubleshooting fixes broken behavior, while tuning improves functioning systems. Good tuning is iterative and conservative — you change one parameter, observe measurable effects, then proceed. A common concrete example is reducing swapping by lowering the vm. swappiness value so the kernel prefers R A M for active data, improving interactive performance. A frequent misconception is that lower values are always better; in low-memory or multi-tenant systems, some swapping can be preferable. Always back up current settings and test in a staging environment when possible. Key takeaway: measure first, change one thing, and verify results. Which single metric would you choose to judge improvement on your server?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Tuning is an iterative, measurement-driven process: change one variable, measure its effect, and revert if it harms performance.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is performance tuning?

An iterative, measurement-led process to improve responsiveness and throughput without breaking the system.

Explanation
  • Measure baseline metrics before making changes using top, free, vmstat, and iostat.
  • Change one parameter at a time to isolate effects and reduce risk.
  • Prefer temporary runtime changes first, then persist when verified.
  • Document the change and have a rollback plan for production systems.
Example
Lower vm.swappiness from 60 to 10 to reduce swapping and keep active application pages in RAM for better responsiveness on systems with ample memory.
Key Takeaway

Tuning is not guesswork: measure, change one thing, re-measure, and persist only after you confirm improvement.

Analogy: Tuning a car engine
Like adjusting timing or mixture, each tuning choice has trade-offs; small incremental changes reduce the chance of harm.
Measure
Use tools to quantify the bottleneck.
Change
Adjust one kernel or process setting.
Verify
Re-run the workload and compare metrics.
Rollback
Revert if performance degrades or instability appears.
Common mistake: changing many parameters at once and assuming a positive result is caused by a specific change.

screens.title: Using sysctl safely
screens.narratorSegment: The sysctl interface lets you view and change kernel parameters at runtime. Start by listing values to discover what you can tune. For example, run a command that lists parameters and filter for swappiness to see the current setting. To test a temporary change, set the parameter at runtime; this affects the running kernel but will revert on reboot. If the change improves behavior, make it persistent by writing the setting into a sysctl. d file or sysctl. conf so it is applied at boot. Always verify after applying a persistent file with a system-wide reload command and then re-check the active value. A concrete example: check the current swappiness, temporarily set it to ten to prefer keeping pages in R A M, run your workload and observe swap usage and latency, and if satisfactory, write vm. swappiness=10 into /etc/sysctl. d/99-swappiness. conf and reload the sysctl configuration. A key misconception is thinking runtime changes are permanent; they are not. Also avoid indiscriminate tuning: understand what a parameter controls before adjusting it. When you persist a parameter, include a short comment in the conf file so others know why the change was made. Which verification command will you run after persisting a change?

keyIdea.title: sysctl workflow
keyIdea.text: Inspect with listing, test with runtime writes, then persist tested values in sysctl.d files and reload to verify.

content.html:
Process Flow

Using sysctl safely

A four-step pattern: inspect, test, persist, verify.

Step-by-step commands
Use these commands to inspect, change, and persist a kernel parameter for testing.
# List all parameters and filter for swappiness
sysctl -a | grep swappiness

# View a specific parameter
sysctl vm.swappiness

# Temporarily set the value (runtime only)
sudo sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10

# Make persistent by writing to sysctl.d and reload
echo "vm.swappiness=10" | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf
sudo sysctl --system

# Verify the active value
sysctl vm.swappiness
Note: Runtime changes revert after reboot; persistent files are applied at boot or via a reload.
Explanation cards
Inspect
Discover current kernel values before changing them.
Test
Apply a runtime change and run the workload to observe effects.
Persist
Write verified values into /etc/sysctl.d/ or sysctl.conf for boot-time application.
Misconception
Don't assume changing many parameters at once is safe; isolate variables so you can attribute effects.
Key Takeaway

Use sysctl for quick experiments and persist only after verification; always include a clear verification step.

screens.title: vm.swappiness explained
screens.narratorSegment: The vm. swappiness parameter controls how aggressively the kernel moves anonymous memory pages from R A M to swap. It is expressed as a value between zero and one hundred: lower values bias towards keeping application data in R A M, while higher values make the kernel more willing to swap. For example, a value of ten makes the kernel prefer R A M and therefore reduces swap activity, which can improve responsiveness for interactive workloads on systems with ample memory. Conversely, a higher default like sixty may be useful on servers with many idle processes where freeing R A M benefits overall throughput. A concrete test is to measure swap usage with free or vmstat before and after lowering swappiness, using a realistic workload that exercises memory pressure. A common misconception is that setting swappiness to zero disables swapping entirely; it only makes swapping much less likely, not impossible. Safety tip: always test in staging and ensure you have sufficient R A M for the intended value. After a verified change, persist it in a sysctl. d file with a short comment explaining the reason. What would your rollback plan be if reducing swappiness caused memory exhaustion?

keyIdea.title: vm.swappiness
keyIdea.text: Controls the kernel's tendency to swap; lower values keep more data in RAM, higher values favor swap to free RAM for active use.

content.html:
Definition

vm.swappiness explained

Understand how the kernel trades RAM for swap and how to test the effect safely.

Meaning and trade-offs
  • 0–10: prefer RAM, reduce swapping; good for interactive systems with ample memory.
  • 40–60: balanced default for many distributions; trades some RAM for lower memory pressure.
  • 80–100: aggressive swapping to free RAM for caches; sometimes useful for specific workloads.
Misconception: setting a low value disables swap — it only reduces swapping frequency, not the mechanism itself.
Concrete example
# Check current value
sysctl vm.swappiness

# Temporarily set to 10
sudo sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10

# Persist the verified value
echo "vm.swappiness=10" | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf
sudo sysctl --system

# Verify with vmstat or free
vmstat 2 5
free -h
Key Takeaway

Test swappiness under real workloads; persist only after confirming the change reduces swap-related latency without causing memory exhaustion.

screens.title: Resource limits: ulimit and limits.conf
screens.narratorSegment: Resource limits prevent a user or process from exhausting system resources. The shell built-in lets you query and set limits for the current shell session and its children; for example, the command to show the maximum number of open files is the one that prints the open-file limit. These temporary changes are useful for testing, but they disappear when the shell exits or the service restarts. For persistent, system-wide, or user-specific limits you use the /etc/security/limits. conf file or a file under /etc/security/limits. d/. There you can set soft and hard limits for items like number of processes or file descriptors for a particular user or group. This is essential for high-concurrency services that need thousands of open files. A common mistake is forgetting to increase the open-file limit for a service that opens many sockets, which results in 'Too many open files' errors. When editing limits. conf, clearly document the reason and restart the service if it reads PAM limits at login or service start. Practice: check the current limit with the shell, raise it temporarily, and then create a persistent entry for the service user; verify by starting the service and checking its effective limits. What persistent limit will you set first for a busy web server?

keyIdea.text: Use ulimit for quick tests and limits.conf for persistent settings; mismatched limits often cause failures under load.

content.html:
Definition

Resource limits: ulimit and limits.conf

Control per-shell and persistent user/group resource limits to prevent resource exhaustion.

Temporary checks with ulimit
# Show current open file limit
ulimit -n

# Temporarily set a new limit for the shell
ulimit -n 10000

# For processes started from this shell the new limit applies
Temporary limits apply only to the shell and its children. Use them for immediate tests.
Persistent limits.conf example
# /etc/security/limits.d/90-web.conf
# Increase open files for web service user
webadmin    soft    nofile  10000
webadmin    hard    nofile  20000

# Increase max processes for a worker group
@webworkers  soft   nproc   4096
@webworkers  hard   nproc   8192
After creating a limits.d file, services that use PAM limits will pick them up at login or service start. Some services read limits on startup, so restart the service to apply.
Key Takeaway

Set persistent limits for service users that need high concurrency and verify by observing the service under realistic load.

screens.title: Prioritizing processes with nice and renice
screens.narratorSegment: nice and renice let you influence the C P U scheduler by setting a process's nice value. The range runs from minus twenty, the highest scheduling priority, to nineteen, the lowest. Starting a non-critical, C P U-heavy job with a high nice value makes it yield C P U to important tasks; for example, start a background batch with a niceness of fifteen so interactive services remain responsive. If a process is already running, renice changes its priority by PID. A concrete hands-on test is to launch a simple infinite loop in the background, check its nice value and C P U consumption with top, then renice it to a lower priority and observe the scheduler's response. A common misconception is that nice reserves C P U — it does not guarantee C P U time, it only biases the scheduler. Be cautious: lowering niceness to negative values requires privilege and can starve other processes if misused. Typical safe practice is to make background batch jobs nicer and reserve negative niceness only for essential services with demonstrated need. After changing priorities, measure the effect on both the target process and the critical services to confirm the change did what you expected. Which process would you make nicer first on your server?

keyIdea.title: nice & renice
keyIdea.text: Use niceness to bias CPU scheduling: raise nice for background jobs, lower it only for critical services and with caution.

content.html:
Process Flow

Prioritizing processes with nice and renice

Adjust process scheduling bias so important services keep responding while heavy jobs run politely in the background.

Commands and example
# Start a process with lower priority (nicer to others)
nice -n 15 my_batch_job.sh &
BG_PID=$!

afterwards, check with top or ps
ps -o pid,ni,cmd -p $BG_PID

# Increase priority (require sudo for negative values)
sudo renice -5 -p $BG_PID

# Lower priority of running process (be polite)
sudo renice 10 -p $BG_PID
Note: positive nice values make a process kinder to others; negative values increase its share and require privileges.
Explanation and checklist
  • Use nice to start a process with a desired scheduling bias.
  • Use renice to change an existing process's nice value by PID or user.
  • Measure CPU usage with top to confirm the scheduler behavior after changes.
  • Avoid setting very negative nice values unless absolutely necessary and authorized.
Key Takeaway

Bias CPU scheduling with nice for non-critical workloads and verify with monitoring tools; negative priorities require caution and privileges.

screens.title: Storage choices and mount options that reduce I/O
screens.narratorSegment: Disk input and output is often the limiting factor for many servers. Choosing faster media like SSDs reduces latency and increases throughput, but correct configuration also matters. A rotating disk under heavy metadata churn will suffer unless you reduce writes. One common, safe mount tweak is noatime, which prevents the kernel from updating a file's access timestamp on every read; this reduces metadata writes on busy filesystems and can noticeably improve performance for read-heavy workloads. Another lever is choosing the right RAID level: RAID 0 boosts throughput at the cost of redundancy, RAID 10 offers both performance and safety for databases, while RAID 1 favors redundancy over speed. Filesystem choice and mount options interact: ext4 with barriers enabled may be safer but slightly slower; XFS often performs well for large files and parallel input and output. A concrete example: mounting a web server document root with noatime can cut write IOPS because static file reads no longer update metadata. A common misconception is that switching to noatime always fixes slow disks; it helps metadata-heavy workloads but won't fix a saturated hardware queue or a failing controller. When tuning disk input and output, measure before and after using tools like iostat and ioping, test in a non-production replica, and rollback if latency or data integrity is affected. What predictable metric will you check first to confirm the change helped?

keyIdea.title: Disk I/O matters
keyIdea.text: Faster media and targeted mount options (like noatime) reduce write pressure and lower latency; always measure and test.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Disk I/O Optimization
Storage & RAID Comparison
Weigh speed, redundancy, and cost
SSD
  • Low latency; better random I/O
  • Good for databases and many small files
  • Higher cost per GB
HDD
  • Higher throughput for large sequential reads
  • Slower random I/O; prone to seek latency
  • Cheaper for bulk storage
Mount Option: noatime
Reduce metadata writes for many read operations
Example fstab line to avoid updating access times:
/dev/sda1 / ext4 defaults,noatime 0 1
Quick takeaway
Key Takeaway

Choose media and mount options for your workload; measure with iostat or ioping before and after any change.

When to change mount options
Concrete guidance and pitfalls

Start by identifying the I/O pattern. If reads dominate and metadata writes spike, noatime can reduce I/O without affecting file contents. For write-heavy transactional databases, prefer journaling-safe settings and consider placing logs on separate devices. If latency is the problem, move to SSDs or tune queues with block device settings.

  • Measure: run iostat -xz 1 5 to view device utilization and average wait times.
  • Test: apply mount change on a test node or remount temporarily with mount -o remount,noatime /.
  • Rollback: keep a script to restore previous fstab entries and remount if latency or errors increase.
Example scenario
A busy static web server uses many small file reads. Remounting the document root with noatime eliminated tens of write IOPS, lowering average disk wait and improving page serving latency. The admin verified the effect with iostat and kept a documented, persistent fstab entry under /etc/fstab.
Common mistake: Enabling noatime on systems that require accurate access times (some backup tools rely on atime). Verify application needs first.

screens.title: Mount flags and filesystem choices — practical examples
screens.narratorSegment: Filesystems are more than a storage format; they come with defaults that affect performance and safety. Ext4, XFS, and Btrfs each have trade-offs. Ext4 is stable and general purpose, XFS scales well for large files and parallel writes, while Btrfs offers advanced features like checksums and snapshots but requires careful management. Mount flags alter behavior: for example, noatime reduces metadata updates, relatime provides a compromise by updating access time only when modified or older, and data=writeback versus data=ordered balance speed and journaling guarantees. A practical example: for a large logging node, using XFS with a separate log device and noatime can improve sustained write throughput. Add to that filesystem-specific tuning flags such as inode sizing and allocation groups to match expected file sizes. A frequent misconception is to treat mount flags as universal performance fixes; in reality they change durability semantics and may break assumptions of backup or monitoring tools. Always run filesystem checks and perform real workload tests. To test changes, create a representative workload with fio or dd that mirrors production input and output. After testing, update fstab for persistence and document why each option was chosen. Which filesystem and flags would you pick for a write-heavy logging server, and why?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Filesystem Tuning
Filesystem summary
Choose by file size and concurrency
ext4
Stable, general purpose, predictable performance for a wide range of workloads.
XFS
Optimized for large files and high concurrency. Good for parallel writes like media or logs.
Btrfs
Advanced features like snapshots and checksums; use with caution and regular maintenance.
Mount flags explained
Balance speed versus metadata accuracy
noatime: Stop updating access times on each read; reduces metadata writes.
relatime: Update atime only if previous atime is older than mtime; safer default compromise.
data=ordered vs data=writeback: Trade journaling safety for speed.
Practical fstab examples
# XFS for large logs, reduced atime updates
/dev/sdb1 /var/log xfs defaults,noatime 0 2

# ext4 for general root filesystem with relatime
/dev/sda1 / ext4 defaults,relatime 0 1
Testing tip: use a small VM or test partition and run fio to simulate production writes before committing fstab changes.
Common mistake: Changing flags on a live filesystem without backups.

screens.title: Memory strategies: swap, THP, and leak detection
screens.narratorSegment: Memory tuning is a balance between keeping hot data in R A M and avoiding excessive swap input and output. Start by observing real usage with free and vmstat; free shows used versus available memory, while vmstat highlights swap in/out activity and memory pressure. If swapping is frequent and you have ample R A M, lowering vm. swappiness reduces the kernel's tendency to move anonymous pages to swap. Transparent hugepages groups adjacent pages into larger blocks which can reduce TLB pressure for some workloads, but they occasionally introduce latency spikes, so enable or disable THP only after testing. For long-running services, memory leaks are a serious source of pressure: use tools such as pmap, smem, or application-specific profilers to track resident memory growth over time. A concrete example: a Java process steadily grows RSS over days; enabling heap dumps and running a profiler shows an unbounded cache; fixing the code eliminated swap churn. A common misconception is that adding swap is a substitute for insufficient R A M; swap helps absorb short spikes but is orders of magnitude slower than R A M. The practical workflow is: observe metrics, reproduce workload in a test environment, change THP or swappiness, and measure impact. Always document changes and prepare a rollback plan. What metric would you watch next time you suspect a memory leak?

keyIdea.text: Use free and vmstat to identify swapping and memory pressure; test THP and swappiness changes before production use.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Memory Strategies
Inspect memory quickly
  • free -h: human-readable view of RAM and swap usage.
  • vmstat 1 5: short snapshot of swap and I/O activity.
  • pmap <PID>: view process memory map and resident set size.
Transparent HugePages (THP)
THP can improve performance for some memory-bound apps by reducing TLB misses. However, it can also cause occasional latency spikes. Toggle THP for experiments and compare application latency and throughput before keeping it enabled.
Practical check: reduce swappiness temporarily
To temporarily lower swap tendency run this command and then monitor swapping metrics:
echo 10 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/swappiness
# Verify with: cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness
Safety note: This change is temporary and resets at reboot; make persistent via /etc/sysctl.d if validated.
Example: finding a leak
A service that grows RSS over days suggests a leak. Collect periodic pmap outputs, compare heap sizes, and run the application's memory profiler to identify the leaking data structure. Fixing the code and restarting the service stopped swap usage spikes.

screens.title: Use top, iostat, and vmstat to find bottlenecks
screens.narratorSegment: Good tuning starts with observation. top gives a live view of C P U and per-process resource usage; look for processes consuming high C P U or showing large resident memory. The ‘NI’ (nice) column shows process priority. iostat reports per-device throughput, utilization, and average service time; high await or high utilization suggests disk bottlenecks. vmstat summarizes memory and paging behavior: watch for non-zero si and so columns, which indicate swap activity; high numbers here mean memory pressure. A concrete workflow: run iostat -xz 1 5 while running the suspected workload to see device saturation, then run top to map saturation back to processes. Use vmstat to confirm whether high input and output is accompanied by swapping. A common misconception is to treat a single metric as definitive; instead correlate multiple tools. For example, high C P U wait time combined with high iowait points toward storage delays, not C P U inefficiency. Another practical tip: capture 60 seconds of data in non-production during expected peak load and compare before/after your tuning change. This evidence-driven approach reduces guesswork and helps justify persistent changes. What two metrics would you correlate to confirm a disk bottleneck?

keyIdea.text: Combine top, iostat, and vmstat outputs to pinpoint whether CPU, memory, or I/O is the root cause.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Monitoring Tools
Live process view: top
Use top to identify CPU-hungry or memory-hungry processes. Note the PID, CPU%, RES, and NI columns. If a process is misbehaving, you can correlate its PID to disk or network I/O with other tools.
# run top and observe PID, %CPU, RES, NI
top -b -n 1 | head -n 20
Device-level view: iostat
iostat shows device utilization, average wait, and throughput. Look for high %util and large await values as indications of saturation.
iostat -xz 1 5
Summarize with vmstat
vmstat helps spot swapping and run queue pressure. si and so columns indicate swap in/out; r reports runnable processes waiting for CPU. Correlate r with %idle and iowait to distinguish CPU waits from I/O waits.
vmstat 1 5
Pro tip: capture several samples during peak activity and save them for before/after comparisons.
Check correlation

screens.title: Iterative tuning: monitor, adjust, verify, document
screens.narratorSegment: Performance tuning is an iterative workflow, not a one-time fix. Begin with careful monitoring to establish a baseline: collect representative metrics during normal and peak load using top, iostat, vmstat, and application logs. Next, form a hypothesis: identify the likely bottleneck and choose a conservative change to test, such as lowering vm. swappiness or remounting with noatime. Apply the change in a test environment or during a maintenance window if testing on production is unavoidable. Then verify by rerunning the same workload and comparing the collected metrics to the baseline. Important: make one change at a time so you can attribute effects. If the result is positive and stable, make it persistent and record the exact commands, file edits, and why the change was made in your system runbook. If it regresses, revert immediately and investigate logs. A common mistake is changing multiple parameters simultaneously or relying on anecdotal improvement without metric-backed evidence. Another misconception is to assume default kernel settings are always suboptimal; defaults are conservative and safe for many workloads. Concrete example: lowering swappiness from 60 to 10 on a web server with lots of R A M reduced swap-in activity and improved latency after validation. Finish each cycle with a brief post-change checklist and a rollback plan. Which test will convince you the change is safe for production?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Tuning Workflow
Steps
  1. Measure baseline with representative load.
  2. Form hypothesis and pick a single, small change.
  3. Test in a staging environment or maintenance window.
  4. Verify metrics and latency after change.
  5. Document, persist, and prepare rollback steps.
Checklist for a safe change
- Capture pre-change metrics and save them with timestamps.
- Notify stakeholders and schedule a short maintenance window if modifying production.
- Apply the change and run the same benchmark or replay traffic.
- Compare before/after graphs and check system logs for errors.
- If success, persist the change; if not, roll back and analyze.
Scenario: reduce swapping safely
An admin measured swap spikes at peak time. They lowered swappiness to 10 on a staging server, replayed peak traffic, and observed lower swap-ins and improved response time. After two days of monitoring, they applied the persistent sysctl file and documented the change and test results in the runbook.
Key Takeaway

A disciplined, metric-driven workflow reduces regression risk and creates an audit trail for system changes.

fullNarratorScript:
Performance tuning is about improving how a system uses its resources so services respond faster and do more work with less waste. In this lesson you will learn what tuning is, how to change kernel parameters safely with the sysctl facility, how to set user and process resource limits, and how to give processes the right C P U priority. Rather than chasing symptoms, tuning should be driven by monitoring: measure first, change one thing at a time, and re-measure. For example, you might reduce swapping by adjusting a kernel setting so interactive applications feel snappier, or raise file-descriptor limits for a busy web server so it can accept many concurrent connections. We will walk through concrete commands, file edits that persist changes across reboots, and a simple experiment that launches a background job and adjusts its priority. I will also point out common pitfalls—like changing a kernel knob without testing—that can cause instability. By the end of the sequence you will know how to make small, reversible changes and validate their effect. Think of tuning as careful engineering rather than guesswork: measure, adjust, verify. What will you measure first on your system?

By the end of this chapter you will understand the practice of performance tuning and be able to apply specific tools to safely change system behavior. First, you will define performance tuning and contrast it with reactive troubleshooting so you can choose measurement-driven changes rather than guesswork. Second, you will use sysctl to inspect and modify kernel parameters temporarily and persistently, with a practical example targeting swap behavior. Third, you will configure user and process resource limits using the shell built-in and limits. conf so services under heavy load do not exhaust file descriptors or processes. Finally, you will control C P U scheduling priority with nice and renice to ensure important services remain responsive while background tasks run. Each objective emphasizes safety: make a single change, test it, and roll back if needed. These skills let you improve responsiveness, avoid common limit-related failures, and prioritize C P U usage without destabilizing the system. Which observable metric will you measure first on your server?

This lesson focuses on actionable skills: how to inspect current kernel values, make temporary changes for testing, and persist safe values so they survive reboot. You will also practice checking file-descriptor limits and applying persistent per-user limits for services that need many open files. For C P U management, you will learn to launch jobs with lower priority so they don't interfere with interactive workloads, and to raise priority for critical processes using renice. Each action includes verification: use sysctl to read the active value, run top or ps to observe priority, and test service behavior under simulated load. We'll walk through a hands-on scenario where you lower vm. swappiness to reduce swapping, then bring up a background C P U-bound loop and adjust its nice value to see scheduling effects. The emphasis is on repeatable steps: change one variable at a time, measure with top, free, and iostat, and document results so you can revert if necessary. What metric will show you that swapping has decreased after a change?

Performance tuning is the deliberate practice of adjusting configuration and resource allocations to improve responsiveness, throughput, or efficiency. A helpful analogy is tuning a car engine: you measure how it runs, adjust a single setting like timing or fuel mixture, test the change on a drive, and then decide whether to keep it. In Linux that single setting might be a kernel parameter, a per-user limit, or a process priority. Tuning differs from troubleshooting: troubleshooting fixes broken behavior, while tuning improves functioning systems. Good tuning is iterative and conservative — you change one parameter, observe measurable effects, then proceed. A common concrete example is reducing swapping by lowering the vm. swappiness value so the kernel prefers R A M for active data, improving interactive performance. A frequent misconception is that lower values are always better; in low-memory or multi-tenant systems, some swapping can be preferable. Always back up current settings and test in a staging environment when possible. Key takeaway: measure first, change one thing, and verify results. Which single metric would you choose to judge improvement on your server?

The sysctl interface lets you view and change kernel parameters at runtime. Start by listing values to discover what you can tune. For example, run a command that lists parameters and filter for swappiness to see the current setting. To test a temporary change, set the parameter at runtime; this affects the running kernel but will revert on reboot. If the change improves behavior, make it persistent by writing the setting into a sysctl. d file or sysctl. conf so it is applied at boot. Always verify after applying a persistent file with a system-wide reload command and then re-check the active value. A concrete example: check the current swappiness, temporarily set it to ten to prefer keeping pages in R A M, run your workload and observe swap usage and latency, and if satisfactory, write vm. swappiness=10 into /etc/sysctl. d/99-swappiness. conf and reload the sysctl configuration. A key misconception is thinking runtime changes are permanent; they are not. Also avoid indiscriminate tuning: understand what a parameter controls before adjusting it. When you persist a parameter, include a short comment in the conf file so others know why the change was made. Which verification command will you run after persisting a change?

The vm. swappiness parameter controls how aggressively the kernel moves anonymous memory pages from R A M to swap. It is expressed as a value between zero and one hundred: lower values bias towards keeping application data in R A M, while higher values make the kernel more willing to swap. For example, a value of ten makes the kernel prefer R A M and therefore reduces swap activity, which can improve responsiveness for interactive workloads on systems with ample memory. Conversely, a higher default like sixty may be useful on servers with many idle processes where freeing R A M benefits overall throughput. A concrete test is to measure swap usage with free or vmstat before and after lowering swappiness, using a realistic workload that exercises memory pressure. A common misconception is that setting swappiness to zero disables swapping entirely; it only makes swapping much less likely, not impossible. Safety tip: always test in staging and ensure you have sufficient R A M for the intended value. After a verified change, persist it in a sysctl. d file with a short comment explaining the reason. What would your rollback plan be if reducing swappiness caused memory exhaustion?

Resource limits prevent a user or process from exhausting system resources. The shell built-in lets you query and set limits for the current shell session and its children; for example, the command to show the maximum number of open files is the one that prints the open-file limit. These temporary changes are useful for testing, but they disappear when the shell exits or the service restarts. For persistent, system-wide, or user-specific limits you use the /etc/security/limits. conf file or a file under /etc/security/limits. d/. There you can set soft and hard limits for items like number of processes or file descriptors for a particular user or group. This is essential for high-concurrency services that need thousands of open files. A common mistake is forgetting to increase the open-file limit for a service that opens many sockets, which results in 'Too many open files' errors. When editing limits. conf, clearly document the reason and restart the service if it reads PAM limits at login or service start. Practice: check the current limit with the shell, raise it temporarily, and then create a persistent entry for the service user; verify by starting the service and checking its effective limits. What persistent limit will you set first for a busy web server?

nice and renice let you influence the C P U scheduler by setting a process's nice value. The range runs from minus twenty, the highest scheduling priority, to nineteen, the lowest. Starting a non-critical, C P U-heavy job with a high nice value makes it yield C P U to important tasks; for example, start a background batch with a niceness of fifteen so interactive services remain responsive. If a process is already running, renice changes its priority by PID. A concrete hands-on test is to launch a simple infinite loop in the background, check its nice value and C P U consumption with top, then renice it to a lower priority and observe the scheduler's response. A common misconception is that nice reserves C P U — it does not guarantee C P U time, it only biases the scheduler. Be cautious: lowering niceness to negative values requires privilege and can starve other processes if misused. Typical safe practice is to make background batch jobs nicer and reserve negative niceness only for essential services with demonstrated need. After changing priorities, measure the effect on both the target process and the critical services to confirm the change did what you expected. Which process would you make nicer first on your server?

Disk input and output is often the limiting factor for many servers. Choosing faster media like SSDs reduces latency and increases throughput, but correct configuration also matters. A rotating disk under heavy metadata churn will suffer unless you reduce writes. One common, safe mount tweak is noatime, which prevents the kernel from updating a file's access timestamp on every read; this reduces metadata writes on busy filesystems and can noticeably improve performance for read-heavy workloads. Another lever is choosing the right RAID level: RAID 0 boosts throughput at the cost of redundancy, RAID 10 offers both performance and safety for databases, while RAID 1 favors redundancy over speed. Filesystem choice and mount options interact: ext4 with barriers enabled may be safer but slightly slower; XFS often performs well for large files and parallel input and output. A concrete example: mounting a web server document root with noatime can cut write IOPS because static file reads no longer update metadata. A common misconception is that switching to noatime always fixes slow disks; it helps metadata-heavy workloads but won't fix a saturated hardware queue or a failing controller. When tuning disk input and output, measure before and after using tools like iostat and ioping, test in a non-production replica, and rollback if latency or data integrity is affected. What predictable metric will you check first to confirm the change helped?

Performance tuning is an iterative workflow, not a one-time fix. Begin with careful monitoring to establish a baseline: collect representative metrics during normal and peak load using top, iostat, vmstat, and application logs. Next, form a hypothesis: identify the likely bottleneck and choose a conservative change to test, such as lowering vm. swappiness or remounting with noatime. Apply the change in a test environment or during a maintenance window if testing on production is unavoidable. Then verify by rerunning the same workload and comparing the collected metrics to the baseline. Important: make one change at a time so you can attribute effects. If the result is positive and stable, make it persistent and record the exact commands, file edits, and why the change was made in your system runbook. If it regresses, revert immediately and investigate logs. A common mistake is changing multiple parameters simultaneously or relying on anecdotal improvement without metric-backed evidence. Another misconception is to assume default kernel settings are always suboptimal; defaults are conservative and safe for many workloads. Concrete example: lowering swappiness from 60 to 10 on a web server with lots of R A M reduced swap-in activity and improved latency after validation.
